stimulus.t: Some scholars contend that the International Court’s advisory opinions have no practical effect, because such opinions are not legally binding.
But states frequently cite advisory opinions in their diplomatic correspondence when justifying changes in their policies.
Therefore, advisory opinions do have practical effect.

stem: The argument depends on assuming which one of the following?
choices: Advisory opinions ought to be made legally binding.
Advisory opinions are cited in diplomatic correspondence more often than binding judgments are.
At least some of the policy changes that states justify by citing advisory opinions would have been different had those opinions not been issued.
Every advisory opinion the Court has issued has been cited by at least one state.
States never change a policy without citing an advisory opinion in support of the change.

diagram.gap: The citations reflect real influence, not after-the-fact window dressing.

brief.facts: Scholars: non-binding means no effect. Author: states cite the opinions when justifying policy changes, so the opinions have effect.
brief.issue: What must be true for citations to show practical effect?
brief.rule: Negation Test: negate the answer. If the argument collapses, the answer is a necessary assumption.

analysis.correct: (C) Negated: every such policy change would have happened exactly the same way without the opinions. Then the citations are mere decoration and show no practical effect, so the argument collapses.

wrong.label: out-of-scope
wrong.why: What ought to happen is irrelevant to whether the opinions currently have effect.

wrong.label: irrelevant-comparison
wrong.why: The frequency relative to binding judgments does not matter.

wrong.label: too-strong
wrong.why: Some opinions having effect is enough; every opinion need not be cited.

wrong.label: too-strong
wrong.why: The argument needs only SOME influence, not that every policy change cites an opinion.

brief.holding: When evidence is a proxy (citations), the argument assumes the proxy tracks the real thing (influence).

stimulus.t: After the Dalmar Pension Fund replaced its active equity managers with low-cost index funds, its average annual return after fees rose by 1.1 percentage points over the following five years, compared with the previous five.
Clearly, the switch to index funds improved the fund’s performance.

stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?
choices: The fund will continue to earn higher returns as long as it holds index funds.
The rise in the fund’s returns was not due entirely to a general market upswing that would have raised the previous managers’ returns just as much.
Index funds outperform actively managed funds in every five-year period.
Other pension funds that switched to index funds also saw their returns rise.
The fund’s previous managers charged higher fees than any other active managers in the market.

diagram.gap: No other factor (such as a market upswing) fully accounts for the higher returns.

brief.facts: Returns rose after the switch, comparing one five-year period with the previous one. The author concludes that the switch caused the improvement.
brief.issue: What must be true for a before-and-after comparison to show causation?
brief.rule: Causal conclusions assume that no alternative cause fully explains the effect. Necessary-assumption answers often rule out one alternative.

analysis.correct: (B) Negated: the improvement was entirely a market-wide upswing that would have lifted the old managers equally. Then the switch improved nothing, and the argument collapses.

wrong.label: out-of-scope
wrong.why: The future is irrelevant to whether the switch improved past performance.

wrong.label: too-strong
wrong.why: The argument concerns one fund in one period, not every period.

wrong.label: irrelevant-comparison
wrong.why: Helpful corroboration, but not required. The argument survives if other funds had no such experience.

wrong.label: too-strong
wrong.why: The managers need not be the most expensive in the market.

brief.holding: Every ‘X happened, then Y improved, so X caused it’ argument assumes the absence of a fully sufficient alternative cause.

stimulus.t: Linguist: The Mansi and Khanty languages share dozens of words for reindeer-herding equipment that are found in no other Ugric language.
Some researchers hold that these words were borrowed after the two peoples came into contact in recent centuries.
But the shared words display the regular sound changes that each language underwent in its prehistoric period.
So the words were inherited from a common ancestor language rather than recently borrowed.

stem: The linguist’s argument requires the assumption that
choices: words borrowed between the two languages in recent centuries would not display the regular sound changes of the languages’ prehistoric period
reindeer herding was the primary economic activity of the common ancestor’s speakers
sound changes proceed at the same rate in all languages
most words shared by related languages are inherited rather than borrowed
no words have ever been borrowed between Mansi and Khanty

diagram.gap: Recent borrowings could not show prehistoric sound changes.

brief.facts: The shared words show the prehistoric sound changes. The linguist concludes they are inherited, not recent borrowings.
brief.issue: Why would prehistoric sound changes rule out recent borrowing?
brief.rule: Evidence discriminates between hypotheses only if it is MORE likely under one than the other. The argument assumes recent loans would lack the prehistoric changes.

analysis.correct: (A) Negated: recent loans WOULD display the prehistoric sound changes. Then the evidence fits both hypotheses equally, and the argument collapses.

wrong.label: too-strong
wrong.why: The ancestor’s speakers needed only the vocabulary, not herding as their primary economy.

wrong.label: out-of-scope
wrong.why: The rate of change is irrelevant; what matters is whether the changes show up in loans.

wrong.label: too-strong
wrong.why: A general statistical claim the argument does not need.

wrong.label: too-strong
wrong.why: The argument concerns these particular words, not all words ever.

brief.holding: Arguments that choose between two hypotheses assume the evidence is inconsistent with the rejected one.

stimulus.t: The city’s new ordinance allows food trucks to operate only in designated zones.
Since the ordinance took effect, complaints about sidewalk congestion have fallen by half.
So the ordinance has reduced sidewalk congestion.

stem: The argument assumes which one of the following?
choices: Food truck operators support the ordinance.
Residents did not become much less inclined to file complaints about congestion after the ordinance took effect.
Food trucks were the only cause of sidewalk congestion.
The designated zones are not themselves congested.
Complaints about other municipal matters have also fallen.

brief.facts: Complaints about congestion halved after the ordinance. Conclusion: congestion fell.
brief.issue: Complaints are a proxy. What must hold for the proxy to track reality?
brief.rule: Proxy arguments assume the measure (complaints) moves with the thing measured (congestion).

analysis.correct: (B) Negated: residents simply stopped complaining (for example, because they gave up). Then fewer complaints say nothing about congestion.

wrong.label: out-of-scope
wrong.why: Operators’ opinions are irrelevant.

wrong.label: too-strong
wrong.why: Trucks need only contribute to congestion, not be the sole cause.

wrong.label: out-of-scope
wrong.why: The zones could be busy while overall congestion still fell.

wrong.label: irrelevant-comparison
wrong.why: If anything, a general fall in complaints would WEAKEN the argument; it is not assumed.

brief.holding: Whenever a measurement stands in for reality, the argument assumes the measurement was not distorted.

stimulus.t: Any contract that was signed under duress is voidable.
The Pellas–Varga supply contract was signed while Varga’s factory was subject to an illegal blockade organized by Pellas.
Therefore, the Pellas–Varga contract is voidable.

stem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Some contracts signed during blockades are voidable.
Varga would not have signed the contract had there been no blockade.
Any voidable contract was signed under duress.
Any contract signed while one party was subject to an illegal blockade organized by the other party was signed under duress.
Pellas organized the blockade in order to obtain the contract.

chain: Signed under illegal blockade by other party

brief.facts: Duress → voidable. The contract was signed under an illegal blockade by the counterparty. Conclusion: voidable.
brief.issue: What single addition makes the conclusion airtight?
brief.rule: Sufficient Assumption: connect the new term in the premises (the blockade) to the term that triggers the rule (duress).

analysis.correct: (D) Blockade → duress, and duress → voidable. Chained, the conclusion is guaranteed.

wrong.label: wrong-degree
wrong.why: ‘Some’ cannot guarantee that THIS contract is voidable.

wrong.label: wrong-degree
wrong.why: Suggestive of duress, but a counterfactual about signing does not establish legal duress.

wrong.label: reversal
wrong.why: Reverses the stated rule and still does not connect the blockade to duress.

wrong.label: wrong-degree
wrong.why: Bad motive supports duress but does not, by itself, make the blockade duress in law.

brief.holding: SA answers bridge the rogue term in the premise to the rogue term in the conclusion, completely.

stimulus.t: Economist: A currency peg can survive a speculative attack only if the central bank holds foreign reserves exceeding the monetary base.
Tavria’s central bank holds reserves equal to just 60 percent of its monetary base, and a speculative attack on Tavria’s peg is now under way.
So Tavria will be forced to devalue its currency.

stem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the economist’s conclusion to be properly drawn?
choices: Countries whose reserves exceed their monetary base are never forced to devalue.
Speculative attacks usually succeed against pegged currencies.
Tavria’s central bank cannot borrow foreign reserves from other central banks.
If Tavria is forced to devalue its currency, its peg will not have survived the attack.
If Tavria’s peg does not survive the attack, Tavria will be forced to devalue its currency.

brief.facts: Survive → reserves exceed base. Tavria’s reserves do not exceed its base, so (contrapositive) the peg will not survive. Conclusion: forced devaluation.
brief.issue: What links ‘peg will not survive’ to ‘forced to devalue’?
brief.rule: After applying the contrapositive, look for the missing link between the last established term and the conclusion’s term.

analysis.correct: (E) ¬Survive → Devalue completes the chain: reserves fall short, so no survival, so devaluation.

wrong.label: irrelevant-comparison
wrong.why: It concerns countries with ample reserves, which Tavria is not.

wrong.label: wrong-degree
wrong.why: ‘Usually’ cannot guarantee the conclusion.

wrong.label: half-right
wrong.why: It closes one escape route (borrowing reserves) but still does not link peg failure to devaluation.

wrong.label: reversal
wrong.why: Devalue → ¬Survive runs the wrong direction.

brief.holding: Run the given conditional first, then bridge from its output to the conclusion.

stimulus.t: Philosopher: A person who makes a promise knowing that she cannot keep it acts dishonestly.
Dana promised to repay a loan by June, although she knew she would not have the funds by then.
So Dana acted dishonestly.

stem: The philosopher’s conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Anyone who fails to keep a promise has acted dishonestly.
Only people who know they cannot keep a promise act dishonestly in making it.
Dana did not repay the loan by June.
Anyone who knows she will lack the means to keep a promise knows that she cannot keep it.
Making a promise that one cannot keep is always morally wrong.

chain: Knows she will lack the means
diagram.gap: Knowing you’ll lack the funds = knowing you can’t keep the promise.

brief.facts: Promise + knowledge of inability → dishonest. Dana knew she would lack the funds.
brief.issue: Does knowing she would lack the funds count as knowing she cannot keep the promise?
brief.rule: Bridge the premise’s description (‘knew she would not have the funds’) to the rule’s trigger (‘knowing she cannot keep it’).

analysis.correct: (D) Lacking the means → knowing she cannot keep it. Then the rule applies and the conclusion follows.

wrong.label: out-of-scope
wrong.why: We do not know whether Dana failed to repay; the argument concerns making the promise.

wrong.label: reversal
wrong.why: Dishonest → knows: the reverse of what is needed.

wrong.label: out-of-scope
wrong.why: Later failure does not establish what she knew when she promised.

wrong.label: shell-game
wrong.why: ‘Morally wrong’ is not ‘dishonest.’

brief.holding: When the premise and the rule describe the same situation in different words, the SA is the definition that equates them.

stimulus.t: An arbitral award can be enforced in Velstria only if Velstria’s courts recognize it.
Velstria’s courts recognize no award rendered by a tribunal whose members were all appointed by one party.
Therefore, the award in Kessler v. Ostra cannot be enforced in Velstria.

stem: Which one of the following, if assumed, allows the conclusion to be properly inferred?
choices: All the members of the tribunal in Kessler v. Ostra were appointed by Ostra.
Velstria’s courts recognize every award rendered by a tribunal whose members were appointed by both parties.
Velstria’s courts have refused to recognize at least one award in a case involving Ostra.
Some awards rendered by tribunals appointed by one party have been enforced in other states.
The award in Kessler v. Ostra has not been recognized by the courts of any other state.

chain: Not all appointed by one party
diagram.gap: The Kessler tribunal was appointed entirely by one party.

brief.facts: Enforced → Recognized → not appointed entirely by one party. Conclusion: the Kessler award cannot be enforced.
brief.issue: Which fact triggers the contrapositive for the Kessler award?
brief.rule: To conclude ¬A from A → B → C, establish ¬C for the case at hand.

analysis.correct: (A) An entirely one-party tribunal means no recognition, and no recognition means no enforcement. The conclusion follows.

wrong.label: irrelevant-comparison
wrong.why: Describes when awards ARE recognized, which does not show this one is not.

wrong.label: wrong-degree
wrong.why: One refusal in some other Ostra case says nothing about this award.

wrong.label: out-of-scope
wrong.why: Other states are irrelevant to enforcement in Velstria.

wrong.label: out-of-scope
wrong.why: Only Velstria’s courts matter.

brief.holding: For an SA that defeats an outcome, supply the fact that fails the chain’s final necessary condition.

stimulus.t: After the Harbor Authority installed new automated cranes, the average time that cargo ships spent docked fell by 20 percent.
The Authority concludes that the cranes caused the reduction.

stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in evaluating the Authority’s conclusion?
choices: whether the average size of the cargo ships using the harbor changed after the cranes were installed
whether other harbors have also installed automated cranes
how much the cranes cost to purchase and install
whether the Authority plans to install additional cranes
whether the cranes were manufactured domestically

diagram.gap: Nothing else (such as smaller ships) explains the shorter docking times.

brief.facts: Docking time fell 20% after the new cranes. The Authority concludes that the cranes caused it.
brief.issue: What question has an answer that would strengthen OR weaken the causal claim?
brief.rule: Evaluate answers pose a question with two possible answers, one helping and one hurting. Alternative causes are prime candidates.

analysis.correct: (A) If ships got smaller, smaller loads could explain shorter stays (weakens). If ship size was unchanged, that alternative is ruled out (strengthens).

wrong.label: irrelevant-comparison
wrong.why: Without data on those harbors’ docking times, this tells us nothing.

wrong.label: out-of-scope
wrong.why: Cost has no bearing on causation.

wrong.label: out-of-scope
wrong.why: Future plans do not bear on past causation.

wrong.label: out-of-scope
wrong.why: Where the cranes were made is irrelevant.

brief.holding: Run the Variance Test: answer the question both ways. If the two answers push the argument in opposite directions, it is the Evaluate answer.

stimulus.t: Fund manager: Our emerging-markets equity fund has outperformed its benchmark index in each of the past three years.
This shows that our stock selection adds value for our investors.

stem: Which one of the following would it be most useful to determine in order to evaluate the fund manager’s argument?
choices: whether the benchmark index itself rose in each of the past three years
whether other emerging-markets funds charge higher fees
whether the fund manager holds an advanced degree in finance
whether the fund’s investors were satisfied with its returns
whether the fund achieved its outperformance by taking on substantially more risk than its benchmark carries

diagram.gap: Outperformance came from stock selection rather than from extra risk.

brief.facts: The fund beat its benchmark three years running. The manager credits stock selection.
brief.issue: What would distinguish skill in selection from other sources of excess return?
brief.rule: Excess return can come from skill, luck, or bearing more risk. Evaluate answers often probe the leading alternative explanation.

analysis.correct: (E) If the fund simply took much more risk (higher beta, leverage, concentration), higher returns in rising markets reflect risk, not selection skill. If not, the manager’s claim gains support.

wrong.label: irrelevant-comparison
wrong.why: Outperformance is relative to the benchmark, whatever the benchmark’s direction.

wrong.label: irrelevant-comparison
wrong.why: Other funds’ fees say nothing about this fund’s selection skill.

wrong.label: out-of-scope
wrong.why: Credentials do not establish where returns came from.

wrong.label: out-of-scope
wrong.why: Satisfaction does not bear on the source of returns.

brief.holding: For performance claims, ask: was it skill, luck, or risk?

stimulus.t: Political scientist: Countries that adopted proportional representation in the 1990s have since seen voter turnout decline less than countries that retained single-member districts.
Hence, adopting proportional representation helps sustain voter turnout.

stem: In order to evaluate the political scientist’s argument, it would be most useful to know
choices: whether turnout in the countries that adopted proportional representation was already declining more slowly than elsewhere before they adopted it
whether proportional representation tends to produce more stable governments
whether voters in countries with single-member districts prefer their electoral system
whether turnout is generally higher in national elections than in local elections
whether any country has adopted proportional representation since the 1990s

diagram.gap: The slower decline began with the reform, not before it.

brief.facts: PR adopters saw turnout fall less than non-adopters. The author concludes that PR helps sustain turnout.
brief.issue: Is the difference caused by PR, or was it there all along?
brief.rule: A pre-existing trend is a classic alternative explanation for a before-and-after or between-group difference.

analysis.correct: (A) If adopters were already declining more slowly before adopting PR, the difference predates the reform (weakens). If the slowdown began only after adoption, causation is more credible (strengthens).

wrong.label: out-of-scope
wrong.why: Government stability is a different outcome.

wrong.label: out-of-scope
wrong.why: Voter preferences about the system do not bear on turnout causation.

wrong.label: irrelevant-comparison
wrong.why: The national-versus-local difference is unrelated to the comparison at issue.

wrong.label: out-of-scope
wrong.why: Later adopters do not bear on whether PR caused the observed difference.

brief.holding: Before crediting a reform, check the trend line that preceded it.
